intro.title: About Reports
intro.body: Here you see the numbers management and auditors ask for first: **overdue deadlines** in every area, **open deviations and findings**, and how the figures have **developed** month by month. Requirement coverage per standard is under **Standards and requirements**. Everything follows your access: you only see figures for records you can read.
steps: Choose a standard at the top to see only its figures, or keep «All standards».
Start with the overdue deadlines. Choose «Create task» to share out the follow-up.
Use «Write the text» for a short status for management review, and read it through before you share it.

why.body: Every ISO management-system standard asks the organisation to **monitor, measure, analyse and evaluate** its results (clause 9.1), and to bring the results and **trends** to **management review** (9.3). One overview that is always up to date means those inputs are ready when you need them.

intro.title: Every deadline in one place
intro.body: The organisation calendar shows every open deadline you can see, from every area: tasks, document reviews, deviations and actions, audits, contract renewals, supplier evaluations, training expiry and more. The colour shows what the deadline needs.
steps: Move between months, or switch to the list view.
Choose «My deadlines» to see what you are responsible for, or an area to plan one part of the system.
Choose «Create task» on a deadline to share out the follow-up, or add the calendar to your own with the .ics button.

why.body: Planned activities only work if someone does them on time (clause 8.1). With every deadline in one view you can share out the work, avoid clashes with audits and reviews, and show an auditor that planned actions are followed up.

empty.title: Nothing is due in this period
empty.body: When tasks, reviews or actions get deadlines, they show here. Try another month or area, or tick «Include older overdue deadlines».

intro.title: Download the registers the auditor asks for
intro.body: A register is a list of records of one type: risks, legal requirements, deviations, corrective actions, documents, training, suppliers, assets, audits, the records of processing, AI systems and more. Each register shows which requirements it is evidence for.
steps: Narrow it down with filters and columns. The preview shows exactly what the file will hold.
Download, or choose «Save as report» to run the same thing again later.

why.body: The standards ask for **documented information** to be available and suitable for use when it is needed (clause 7.5). Registers you can download on demand let you answer an auditor's request in minutes, with a file that shows exactly what is recorded.

empty.title: No registers are available to you
empty.body: Registers come from the modules you can read. Ask an administrator to switch on the modules you need, or to give you access to them.

standard.help: Requirement registers, such as the Statement of Applicability (SoA) and the evidence index, are made for one standard at a time.
standard.example: ISO 27001 gives the Statement of Applicability with the Annex A controls.

intro.title: Reports you run again in one click
intro.body: A saved report remembers a register with its filters, columns, format and language. Run it when you need a fresh copy, or schedule it so someone gets a reminder. Every run is saved, and becomes evidence that the organisation monitors its results.
steps: Create a report here, or use «Save as report» on the registers page.
Open a report to run it or schedule it.
Under «Runs» you see who ran the report, and when.

why.body: Results only become comparable when you measure the same thing the same way over time (clause 9.1). Saved reports keep the method fixed, so the figures for management review mean the same every time.

empty.title: No saved reports yet
empty.body: Save the registers you download regularly, for example open deviations for the monthly quality meeting, or overdue tasks for management review.

intro.title: What should the report hold?
intro.body: Choose the register, then filters and columns. You only see the filters the register supports. Leave the columns as they are to include all of them.

why.body: A report with a clear name and description tells colleagues what it measures and why, so it stays useful when people change roles.

register.help: The list of records the report reads. The register cannot be changed later. Create a new report for another register.
register.example: Corrective actions for the quality meeting, or the risk register for management review.

format.help: The format used when you choose «Run the report». You can always run it in the other formats too.
format.example: PDF to share with management, Excel for further analysis.

changeReason.help: A short note on why you changed the report. It shows in the change history.

intro.title: Run, schedule and follow up the report
intro.body: Run the report in the format you want. Each run is saved with who, when, the number of rows and a checksum. Schedule it to get a recurring task, which closes when the report is run.

why.body: Recording when a report was run, and by whom, is evidence that monitoring happens as planned (clause 9.1), and gives input to management review (9.3).

leadDays.help: How many days before each run the task appears for the person responsible.
leadDays.example: 3 days gives time to prepare the monthly meeting.

intro.title: Everything the auditor asks for, in one file
intro.body: An audit pack is a zip file for one or more standards: a table of contents, the Statement of Applicability (SoA), the evidence index, requirement coverage, approved policies and the registers an auditor expects, such as the risk assessment, internal audits, management review, competence and suppliers. A checksum per file later shows the pack is unchanged.
steps: Choose «Create audit pack» and the standards. Link the pack to the audit it is for, if there is one.
Check the ticked registers, and whether policies go in.
Download the zip file and send it to the auditor, or keep it as a snapshot.

why.body: Internal and external audits (clause 9.2) go faster when the evidence is complete and organised. A dated pack with a checksum also shows what the management system looked like at a point in time (clause 7.5).

empty.title: No audit packs yet
empty.body: Create a pack before an internal audit, a certification audit or a customer assessment. It only takes a moment.

standard.help: Only standards switched on for the organisation can be included. The pack holds what you have access to right now.
standard.example: ISO 27001 and GDPR in one pack before a customer audit.

audit.help: The audit the pack is made for. The pack then shows on the audit, and the audit's standards are chosen.

period.help: The period the pack covers, for example the audit year. It is written in the table of contents.

intro.title: What the pack holds
intro.body: Here you see the requirement coverage per standard when the pack was made, the audit it is for, and every file in the zip. The checksum identifies exactly this pack. Recompute it for the downloaded file to show nothing has changed.

why.body: Documented information must be protected against unintended changes (clause 7.5.3). The checksum and the stored copy let you show exactly what the auditor received.

intro.title: Give each role the key numbers it needs
intro.body: Choose the cards shown under «Key numbers for your role» on the Reports page. There are ready-made layouts for the quality manager, information security manager, data protection officer, health and safety manager and auditor, among others. A layout you save for a role comes first.
steps: Choose «The whole organisation» or a role.
Add, order and resize the cards. Choosing a standard on a card shows only its figures.
Save. «Reset» removes the layout, so the next one in line applies again.

why.body: Top management makes sure the management system achieves its intended results (clause 5.1). When each role sees the figures it is responsible for, attention stays on what matters.

scope.help: Layouts marked «(customised)» are saved for that role. Cards whose data someone cannot see show as unavailable to them.

measuring-compliance.title: Measuring how your management system performs

sections.heading: What clause 9.1 asks for
sections.body: You decide **what** to monitor and measure, **how** and **when**, and **when the results are analysed**. The point is not to collect numbers but to know whether your processes work and your objectives are met.

sections.heading: Leading and lagging indicators
sections.body: Open findings and incidents tell you what already went wrong (lagging). Overdue actions, reviews not done and training not completed warn you before it goes wrong (leading). A good overview has both.

sections.heading: From figures to decisions
sections.body: Bring the results to management review (9.3) with a short explanation: what changed, why, and what you propose. The written status is a starting point. Always check it against the figures.

quiz.question: Which of these is a leading indicator?
options: Number of customer complaints last quarter
quiz.explanation: Overdue actions warn you that problems may not be fixed in time, before they show up as complaints or nonconformities.

quiz.question: Where do monitoring results go, according to the ISO structure?
quiz.explanation: Clause 9.3 lists the results of monitoring and measurement as an input to management review.

sections.heading: Records versus documents
sections.body: Documents say what you intend to do (a procedure). **Records** prove what you did (a closed deviation, a completed task). Registers are lists of records, and auditors sample from them.

sections.heading: Export what you can defend
sections.body: An export contains only what you are allowed to see. Use filters to answer the actual question — "all deviations closed this year" — rather than sending everything.

quiz.question: What is a record?
options: Evidence of an activity that was carried out
quiz.explanation: Records are retained documented information that shows results achieved or activities performed.

audit-ready.title: Getting audit-ready with an audit pack

sections.heading: What auditors look at first
sections.body: The **scope**, the **Statement of Applicability** (for ISO 27001), the **policies**, and evidence that requirements are met. An audit pack bundles these so the auditor can plan their sampling.

sections.heading: Check requirement coverage before you send
sections.body: Look at the requirement coverage and the number of requirements without evidence. Gaps you know about and are working on are fine — say so. Gaps you did not know about are what auditors find.

sections.heading: Keep the pack as a snapshot
sections.body: Each pack is stored with a checksum. Months later you can show exactly what you handed over, which helps when findings are discussed.

quiz.question: Why does each pack have a SHA-256 checksum?
options: To prove the pack has not changed since it was generated
quiz.explanation: A checksum changes if a single byte changes, so matching checksums show the file is identical.

overview.title: Look at one standard
overview.body: Choose a standard to see only its deadlines, deviations and trends.

overview.title: The key numbers
overview.body: Overdue deadlines, open deviations and findings, and overdue tasks. Each number shows the change since last month and opens the list behind it.

overview.title: A short written status
overview.body: Have the numbers written up as a short text for management, an auditor or staff. Read it through before you share it.

definitions.title: Save a report
definitions.body: Choose the register, filters and columns once, and run the report again whenever you need it.

auditPacks.title: An audit pack in one click
auditPacks.body: Choose the standards, and the audit if there is one, and download a zip with the Statement of Applicability, the evidence index, registers and policies.

audit-pack.definition: A dated, checksummed bundle of the documented information an auditor needs for one or more standards.

readiness-score.definition: The share of a standard's applicable requirements that have confirmed evidence, from 0 to 100 %.

register.definition: A list of records of one type, such as deviations or documents, that can be filtered and downloaded.
